title: Writing With Machines and Peers: Designing for Critical Engagement with Generative AI
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students engage with generative AI and peer feedback during academic writing, and how they develop reflective relationships with both human and AI reviewers. The central problem is that although generative AI is increasingly used in education, there is limited classroom-based evidence showing how students actually use AI feedback across iterative writing processes, especially alongside peer review.

The study investigates an 8-week pedagogical design in which students in a graduate-level educational technologies course developed literature review or landscape review papers through multiple drafts. Students first received feedback from a custom AI reviewer, CyberScholar, which used rubric-aligned generative AI feedback and follow-up chat. They then revised and received structured peer feedback using the same rubric, followed by additional revision and reflection. Data included AI log files, draft versions, peer reviews, and written reflections, and the authors combined descriptive quantitative analyses with qualitative thematic analysis.

Participants were 10 consenting students from a single graduate course at a large research university in the United States, most of them doctoral students in social-science-related fields. The context was a classroom course hosted in a learning management system, with synchronous discussions, AI-supported review, peer review, and reflective writing. The study focused on authentic academic writing tasks rather than experimental comparison of outcomes across groups.

The main conclusion is that students used AI and peer feedback in complementary ways. AI was primarily valued for rapid, rubric-aligned, surface-level, and organizational feedback, while peer feedback was more useful for conceptual development, disciplinary relevance, and dialogic clarification. Students varied substantially in depth of AI engagement: some used the system transactionally as a scoring/checklist tool, whereas others engaged critically and strategically. The authors argue that hybrid human-AI feedback designs can support writing development, AI literacy, and critical engagement, but that meaningful outcomes depend on pedagogical scaffolding and students’ ability to evaluate and selectively use AI feedback.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small mixed-methods qualitative/case study in higher education with descriptive revision metrics and no control group, randomization, or causal identification. It provides useful implementation evidence but meets only limited credibility criteria for causal claims.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear positive impact on writing development and critical AI engagement, without reported effect sizes or rigorous comparison. Impact is therefore best characterized as positive but uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Custom GPT-4o-based rubric-aligned writing feedback system (CyberScholar/CyberReview) used to review graduate students’ literature-review drafts, score rubric dimensions, provide actionable revision suggestions, and support follow-up dialogue about revisions.
Conversational follow-up chat with the GenAI reviewer to clarify feedback, request examples, negotiate revision decisions, and ask questions about academic writing moves during iterative drafting.
Generative AI used for surface-level writing support such as grammar correction, wording improvement, coherence, and rubric-aligned academic writing refinement.

finding.finding_summary: In this 8-week mixed-methods case study with 10 graduate students, the hybrid AI-plus-peer feedback design was reported to support writing development across iterative drafts, with students using AI mainly for rubric alignment and surface-level edits and peers for conceptual development and disciplinary relevance. Revision analyses showed substantial text changes for several students across draft stages, but no standardized writing gain, inferential statistical test, or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student writing artifacts across three draft versions, revision trajectory metrics (Jaccard similarity; added/deleted n-grams), peer feedback, reflections, and AI chat logs

finding.finding_summary: The study found evidence of improved critical engagement with AI, reflective decision-making, and strategic use of different feedback sources among 10 graduate students. Qualitative cases showed that some students evaluated AI suggestions, negotiated whether to adopt them, and used peers for epistemic validation, indicating growth in metacognition and critical AI literacy, though effects were descriptive rather than statistically estimated.
finding.measure: Reflection notes, AI chat histories coded for depth of engagement, thematic analysis of revision decisions and feedback uptake

finding.finding_summary: Student reflections suggested increasing confidence and comfort in using AI over time, alongside appreciation for the encouragement and affective support provided by peers. The evidence indicates positive shifts in students’ perceived confidence and relational stance toward AI, but these findings were qualitative and no validated socio-emotional scale or effect estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Student written reflections about confidence, encouragement, and evolving relationships with AI and peers
